standard.title: Effects of WWI on Australian Society
standard.description: the effects of the First World War on Australian society, such as the role of women, political debates about conscription, relationships with the British Empire, and the experiences of returned soldiers
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have studied WWI causes (AC9HH9K08), theatres and experiences (AC9HH9K09), and turning points (AC9HH9K10). They understand the nature of the war and the conditions of service. This descriptor shifts focus to the home front — examining how the war transformed Australian society, politics, and international relationships.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students investigate the effects of the First World War on Australian society, including the role of women, conscription debates, Australia-Britain relations, and the experiences of returned soldiers.

nodes.label: Changing roles of women during the war
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can investigate the changes to women's roles during the war and assess what was retained after the war ended.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe at least two changes to women's roles in Australia during WWI.
nodes.typical_width: Investigate examples of women's changed roles during the war (workforce entry, nursing, political activism, managing farms and businesses); compare these wartime roles with women's pre-war roles; examine what changed and what reverted after the war — assessing which changes were temporary and which had lasting effects.
wider: Examine the experiences of Australian nurses on the Western Front or in other theatres — using primary sources to investigate their working conditions, the dangers they faced, and how their service was recognised
Compare women's wartime workforce participation in Australia with that in Britain or France — assessing whether wartime economic necessity produced similar gender role changes internationally
Investigate women's pacifist activism during WWI — examining figures like Vida Goldstein's peace activism — and assess how opposing the war created a different kind of women's political engagement

response_modes.reason: Examining multiple dimensions of women's wartime experience (workforce, nursing, political activism, pacifism) prevents a single-narrative picture and supports genuine analysis of continuity and change.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Women's wartime roles offer a rich lens for examining the relationship between emergency social conditions and structural gender change — how crises open spaces that may or may not close when the crisis ends. This connects to broader contemporary questions about gender and work.
success_criteria: Describes at least two specific changes to women's roles during WWI with historical examples
Assesses whether at least one change was permanent or temporary after the war

nodes.label: Conscription debates and social division
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can investigate the first and second conscription referenda, including the role of Billy Hughes, divisions within the Labor Party, and the groups and grounds for opposition.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe the conscription debate in Australia during WWI and explain who opposed conscription and why.
nodes.typical_width: Investigate the first and second referenda on conscription (1916, 1917); examine the role of Prime Minister Billy Hughes in championing conscription; describe the division within the Labor Party; identify and explain the groups who opposed conscription (trade unionists, Irish Catholics including Archbishop Mannix) and their grounds for opposition; explain why conscription was defeated both times.
wider: Examine the conscription campaign and anti-conscription campaign as uses of propaganda and public persuasion — analysing the specific arguments, imagery, and emotional appeals used by each side
Investigate Archbishop Daniel Mannix's role in the anti-conscription campaign as an example of how religious, ethnic (Irish Catholic), and political identities intersected in Australian public life

Compare Australia's voluntary system with the compulsory systems of Britain, France, and New Zealand — assessing what the conscription debates reveal about Australian national identity and its relationship to the British Empire
nodes.hinge_reason: The conscription debate is the major political fracture of Australian WWI society. Understanding it — who fought it, what was at stake, and why it was defeated twice — is essential for understanding both the war's social effects (Node 3, Node 4) and Australia's changing relationship with Britain.

response_modes.reason: The conscription debate involves multiple actors with different motivations — Billy Hughes, Labor Party, trade unions, Irish Catholics, women pacifists. Examining at least two opposition groups with different grounds gives students a richer understanding than reducing it to a single faction.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The conscription debates are a rich case study in how a national crisis revealed and deepened existing social divisions — class, religion, ethnicity, and imperial loyalty all intersected. Students can trace how political identities formed and fractured under wartime pressure.
success_criteria: Describes the two conscription referenda and their outcomes
Identifies at least two groups that opposed conscription and explains the specific grounds for each group's opposition

nodes.label: Australia-Britain relationship and returned soldiers
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can examine the continuities and changes in Australia's relationship with the British Empire, and explain the effects of war on returned soldiers including First Nations soldiers.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe at least two effects of the war on returned soldiers; describe one way Australia's relationship with Britain changed as a result of the war.
nodes.typical_width: Examine the continuities and changes in Australia's relationship with the British Empire — changing sentiments about Britain as 'mother country', growing sense of independent Australian identity (Gallipoli as nation-defining); explain the effects of war on returned soldiers including physical and psychological trauma, shell shock, employment difficulties, social and racial discrimination, service recognition, land allocation (Soldier Settlement Scheme), wage inequality, and access to health care.
wider: Examine the specific experiences of First Nations Australian returned soldiers — their exclusion from the Soldier Settlement Scheme, wage inequality, access to repatriation services — and assess how racial discrimination compounded the difficulties of returned service

Investigate the Soldier Settlement Scheme as a case study in post-war social policy — examining its intention, its implementation, and why many settler farmers failed — connecting policy design to lived outcomes
Examine how Gallipoli became the founding myth of Australian national identity and assess what this reveals about how nations construct their self-image through selective memory of trauma and heroism

response_modes.reason: This node integrates the wartime experience (AC9HH9K09) with the home-front social effects, connecting what soldiers experienced overseas with how they were treated and what they found on return. Students should draw explicit connections between these.

success_criteria: Explains at least three distinct effects of the war on returned soldiers, including at least one relating to First Nations soldiers
Describes how Australia's relationship with the British Empire changed as a result of the war
